title: Short Stuff: Safety Coffins
summary: Short Stuff episode on safety coffins, devices patented from the 1790s onward to let a buried-alive person signal or escape. The hosts open with George Washington's reported request not to be entombed for three days, then discuss taphephobia (fear of being buried alive), the Romantic and spiritualist context of the period, and Edgar Allan Poe's 1844 story "The Premature Burial." They cover specific devices and showmen: Christian Eisenbrandt's 1843 life-preserving coffin, Franz Wester's escape coffin demonstrations, and Count Michele de Carnice's bell-and-tube casket, including volunteer Faustino Lorenzo's reported nine-day burial in 1898. They close with Timothy Clark Smith's grave window in Vermont, then sign off.
topics: Edgar Allan Poe The Premature Burial

segments.title: Opening banter and George Washington's burial request
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the short stuff and recount George Washington's reported 1799 request not to be entombed for three days after death, which leads to the risk of being buried alive.

segments.title: Checking for death and taphephobia
segments.summary: Discussion of how death was checked before modern medical tools and the question of when pulse checks began. They note that the fear of being buried alive, known as taphephobia, was outsized relative to how often it happened.

segments.title: Origins of safety coffins and romanticism
segments.summary: Safety coffin patents date to the 1790s in Central Europe, according to a historian at the US Patent and Trademark Office. The hosts link their appearance to Romanticism and the rise of spiritualism, and mention pop culture examples of being buried alive.

segments.title: Pop culture references and sponsor break
segments.summary: Hosts riff on film and TV depictions of premature burial. They then announce a break.
topics: buried alive in film and TV

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: Short break before the segment continues.

segments.title: Bell and ladder designs and Eisenbrandt's life-preserving coffin
segments.summary: Describes simple bell-pull designs and a tube-and-ladder escape concept. Covers Christian Eisenbrandt's 1843 Baltimore patent for a spring-loaded lid and the practical problems with it.

segments.title: Poe's Premature Burial and corpse movement
segments.summary: Edgar Allan Poe's 1844 story The Premature Burial is cited as adding to public fear. The hosts argue that decomposition movement may explain some reported cases, but not claw marks.

segments.title: Franz Wester and Count de Carnice showmanship
segments.summary: Franz Wester demonstrated an escape coffin with a tube, ladder, and bell in New Jersey. Count de Carnice toured selling his casket, claiming a figure about buried-alive people, and staged burial demonstrations with volunteers, including Faustino Lorenzo's reported nine-day burial in 1898.

segments.title: Timothy Clark Smith's grave window
segments.summary: Timothy Clark Smith's grave in New Haven, Vermont, has a window that once let passersby look down to his face to check for signs of life.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts wrap up the short stuff and the standard iHeartRadio credit is read.
